In Java architecture, choosing between an interface and an abstract class defines how behavioral contracts and object hierarchies are designed. An abstract class represents an 'is-a' relationship, allowing shared state (instance fields), constructors, and a mix of fully implemented methods alongside abstract declarations. It serves as a partial template for tightly related subclasses, carrying a heavier inheritance cost since a Java class can only extend one superclass. Conversely, an interface models a 'can-do' behavioral capability. Historically, interfaces were pure contracts containing only public static final constants and public abstract methods, enabling a form of multiple inheritance of type since a class can implement multiple interfaces.

The landscape of interface design shifted radically with Java 8, which introduced default methods (defender methods) and static methods inside interfaces. Default methods allow developers to inject new functionality—such as streaming APIs like stream() or forEach()—into existing public interfaces without breaking backward compatibility for downstream implementers. Java 9 further evolved interface capabilities by introducing private interface methods. These private helpers (and private static methods) allow multiple default methods within the same interface to share common internal implementation logic without polluting the public API contract or forcing code duplication.

items: Default methods use the 'default' keyword to provide a fallback body, letting implementers override it or inherit it implicitly.
When a class implements two interfaces that both declare the same default method signature, the Java compiler enforces an explicit override to resolve the diamond problem ambiguity.
Private interface methods encapsulate internal helper logic, keeping default method implementations clean and secure from external extension or overriding.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of the diamond problem with Java 8 default methods. If class C implements interface A and interface B, and both define a default method foo(), the compiler will refuse to compile until C explicitly overrides foo() and calls A.super.foo() or B.super.foo(). Additionally, because interfaces cannot hold state, overusing default methods to simulate traits can lead to complex behavior mixing that violates single-responsibility principles.

title: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class? What changed in Java 8 and Java 9 regarding interfaces?
